Hyper Routine-driven NPC Framework separates population, routines, perception and combat, so the same character can follow a schedule, investigate a sound and react to a threat. Key Features Population and routines Automatic populations: configure NPC classes, minimum/maximum counts and respawn rules within a population area. Assigned populations: manage hand-placed guards, vendors or narrative characters through the same lifecycle. Time-driven routines: choose activities according to time and routine data. World targets: resolve tasks through tagged placeables, patrol splines, Smart Objects and interaction targets. Activities: random roaming, spline patrols, item pickup and Smart Object interaction. Perception and reactions Sight and hearing: interpret visible targets and nearby sound. Investigation: move toward or investigate suspicious audio, including sounds behind walls. Team context: use team awareness when evaluating threats and nearby actors. Emotional reactions: support fleeing, cowering, anger and reactive escape behavior. Awareness display: show Neutral, Curious, Suspicious and Alert states through UI driven by the NPC's current perception and highest active threat. Alert handling: separate awareness and target selection from the combat style that uses the result. Combat and extension Combat routines: use State Trees for the selected fighting behavior. Melee behavior: step-out/heavy attacks, dodge rolls and team encounters. Shared character architecture: support humanoid and non-humanoid NPCs. Data authoring: configure routines, perception and combat through tables and data assets. Population tools: use debug controls and forced load/unload to inspect the authored population. Four connected responsibilities Population decides which NPCs exist. Routines decide what they do over time. Perception selects threats and awareness state. Combat executes the fighting style. This separation lets you change one part without redefining the entire character. The example map demonstrates core behaviors rather than every possible combination. This is an advanced framework; familiarity with State Trees and Unreal AI setup will help you adapt it effectively. Routines that adapt to the world Weighted time slots: give each part of the day a selection of weighted tasks and a fallback routine. Evaluate schedules on configured in-game time intervals. Reusable destination rules: match task, target and NPC identifier tags. A guard and a villager can share a task while resolving different eligible places in the world. Occupancy and fallback: respect target occupancy limits, prefer identifier-specific targets and fall back to generic targets or another routine when a place is unavailable. Simple and complex interactions: use lightweight behavior objects for tasks such as sitting or enabling a vendor, and State Tree interaction objects for activities with waiting, branching or multiple steps. Awareness before combat Stealth and obscured vision: visibility modifiers and authored obscured-vision volumes affect how NPCs perceive targets in areas such as cover, bushes or shadows. Actions create suspicion: sensitivity data can react to sound, equipped or used items, damage, kills and stealing, with different responses for friendly and enemy relationships. Investigation can de-escalate: an NPC can move toward a suspicious stimulus and return from alertness when further evidence does not appear. The very detailed documentation. Rated 5 out of 5 Dalcon4 – May 2, 2026 Review from Fab A breath of fresh air in a sea of scripted AI. The Routine-Driven NPC Framework gives your world citizens a genuine sense of purpose — they wake up, go to work, eat, socialize, and sleep on believable daily schedules, all without hand-authored state machines. Setup is dead simple: define a routine, drop NPCs into your level, and watch them inhabit your world. The framework handles interruptions gracefully, so combat, dialogue, or dynamic events never leave an NPC awkwardly frozen mid-task. Performance-conscious design means you can populate entire cities without tanking your frame rate. For anyone building immersive sims, open-world RPGs, or narrative games where the world has to feel alive when the player isn’t looking, this is indispensable. Architecture you can extend Hyper is built around scalable architecture: gameplay tags, structured data, child Blueprints, clean overrides, reusable components, and clear project boundaries. Start fast, grow cleanly Build on the included systems, replace visuals, adjust data, create child Blueprints and connect features without rebuilding the same foundation from scratch. Want to learn more about the Hyper ecosystem, architecture philosophy, workflows, and developer behind it? Read more here and get started ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/docs/getting-started/start-here/ ). How do I add this to my project? + This module is provided as a full project because it includes Gameplay Tags, collision settings, config settings and other project-level dependencies. Use our free Integration Tool ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/product/integration-tool/ ) to prepare the integration. It combines compatible Hyper projects and handles migration and the required project settings. Use matching Unreal Engine versions and compatible Hyper releases. Your own character, GameMode or custom systems may still need to be connected. The Integration Tool walkthrough ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/docs/getting-started/use-the-automatic-integration-tool/ ) explains the setup and what to check in the generated project. Do I need to use other Hyper systems with this? + No. You can use your own systems. Hyper modules are designed around interfaces, abstract classes, shared contracts and dynamic dispatch, so features are not tied to one specific implementation. If a module demonstrates integration with our Inventory, Equipment, Interaction, Movement, NPC or another Hyper system, you can: Use the included Hyper implementation. Replace it with your own system. Use our implementation as a reference for your own integration. The supplied integration shows how the module connects to the rest of a game. You can connect your own implementation through the same interface, abstract class or integration point. For example, Attribute Manager may demonstrate Equipment modifying attributes. That does not mean you must purchase our Equipment System. You can follow the same integration pattern with your own equipment system. The module includes working gameplay and its integration points. Build on the supplied setup or connect your own systems where you want different behavior. See how to adapt a module ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/docs/getting-started/customize-modules/ ) and how the shared data and abstract classes work ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/docs/project-foundations/datamanagement/ ). Where should I put my own changes? + Keep your own Blueprints, UI and data in your project's folder, for example Content/MyProject. Use child Blueprints or replacement components for your custom logic where possible. That keeps your changes separate when you update Hyper. If you edit the original framework files directly, you will need to merge those edits when updating. The folder structure guide ( https://gamesbyhyper.com/docs/project-foundations/folder-structure/ ) explains where everything belongs. Is this a simple enemy AI template for beginners? + This is an advanced framework built around State Trees and perception. Some Blueprint and Unreal AI experience will help. The example map demonstrates the core setup you can build on. What kinds of routines can it support? + Examples include roaming, spline patrols, smart-object interaction, gathering, melee combat, investigating sounds and reactions such as fleeing or cowering.
